03 · Draw and recovery

How can draw reach 170%?

A ring's blasted tonnes provide the reference quantity. Material arriving at its drawpoint can also include ore left from earlier mining and waste carried through the cave. Total material drawn can therefore exceed that reference quantity.

Draw factor
Total material drawn ÷ reference ring tonnes × 100%.
Current-ring ore recovery
Ore recovered from the current ring ÷ original ore tonnes in that ring × 100%.

A 100-tonne ring example

90 t from the current ring + 50 t of older ore + 30 t of waste = 170 t drawn.

Draw factor = 170%.
Current-ring ore recovery = 90%.

The particles illustrate mixing and downward cave flow. This is a teaching example, rather than a calibrated prediction of this mine's cave.

What the group should keep in mind

The first three levels use target draw factors of 30%, 40% and 50% in the current project cases. These percentages control scheduled tonnes; the ten-percentage-point increase is a project assumption.

Planning assumptions still to confirm
  • Physical cave-front alignment: the two–three-ring neighbour stagger and five-ring upper/lower release compare ring order. Unequal drive lengths require a Deswik position check before accepting those physical offsets.
  • Truck capacity: the unit and time basis of the 217.9 productivity benchmark, the meaning of the 3.52 km haul distance, and actual truck cycle times remain unconfirmed.
  • Hold time: 12 and 24 hours are planning buffers after target draw completion. Readiness for the next ring also depends on preparation, firing windows and operational release.
  • Development readiness: the first three levels are assumed developed, equipped, commissioned and ready before the first production day.
  • Shared haulage: development and western-orebody haulage reservations are currently zero. Their overlapping demand will need to be included later.

Further reading: Campbell, draw-control review (2022) · Hronsky et al., Carrapateena production simulation (2020).
